nodes.name: Propositional Equivalence Law
nodes.question: State the definition: Propositional Equivalence Law.
nodes.statement_display:
A propositional equivalence law is a valid schema of the form
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi,
\]
with \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\). Each instance of the schema says that the two formulas have the same truth value under every truth assignment.
nodes.statement_tex:

\[
\operatorname{PropositionalEquivalenceLaw}(\varphi,\psi)
\]
means that \(\varphi\equiv\psi\) is a valid logical-equivalence schema.
nodes.formal:

\Longleftrightarrow

\land

nodes.source_text: Equivalence laws are the algebraic rewrite rules of propositional logic. They allow formulas to be transformed without changing truth conditions.

nodes.name: Logical Equivalence is an Equivalence Relation
nodes.question: State the theorem: Logical Equivalence is an Equivalence Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
Logical equivalence is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive on \(\WFF\):
\[
\varphi\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\equiv\psi\Longrightarrow\psi\equiv\varphi,
\]
and
\[
(\varphi\equiv\psi\land\psi\equiv\chi)
\Longrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\chi.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Logical equivalence is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive on \(\WFF\):
\[
\varphi\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\equiv\psi\Longrightarrow\psi\equiv\varphi,
\]
and
\[
(\varphi\equiv\psi\land\psi\equiv\chi)
\Longrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\chi.
\]

 \hyperref[prf:logical-equivalence-equivalence-relation]{Go to proof.}
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)(\varphi\equiv\varphi),\\
&(\forall\varphi,\psi\in\WFF)(\varphi\equiv\psi\to\psi\equiv\varphi),\\
&(\forall\varphi,\psi,\chi\in\WFF)
((\varphi\equiv\psi\land\psi\equiv\chi)\to\varphi\equiv\chi).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)(\varphi\equiv\varphi),\\
&(\forall\varphi,\psi\in\WFF)(\varphi\equiv\psi\to\psi\equiv\varphi),\\
&(\forall\varphi,\psi,\chi\in\WFF)
((\varphi\equiv\psi\land\psi\equiv\chi)\to\varphi\equiv\chi).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text: Logical equivalence behaves like equality at the semantic level.

nodes.name: Basic Boolean Equivalence Laws
nodes.question: State the theorem: Basic Boolean Equivalence Laws.
nodes.statement_display:
For all formulas \(\varphi,\psi,\chi\in\WFF\), the following logical equivalences hold.

Commutativity:
\[
\varphi\land\psi\equiv\psi\land\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\psi\equiv\psi\lor\varphi.
\]

Associativity:
\[
(\varphi\land\psi)\land\chi
\equiv
\varphi\land(\psi\land\chi),
\qquad
(\varphi\lor\psi)\lor\chi
\equiv
\varphi\lor(\psi\lor\chi).
\]

Idempotence:
\[
\varphi\land\varphi\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]

Double negation:
\[
\neg\neg\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]

\varphi\land\varphi\equiv\varphi,\quad
\varphi\lor\varphi\equiv\varphi,\quad

\end{gathered}

nodes.name: Identity and Domination Laws
nodes.question: State the theorem: Identity and Domination Laws.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\top\) be any tautological formula and let \(\bot\) be any contradictory formula. Then for every \(\varphi\in\WFF\):
\[
\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi,
\]
and
\[
\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\top\) be any tautological formula and let \(\bot\) be any contradictory formula. Then for every \(\varphi\in\WFF\):
\[
\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi,
\]
and
\[
\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top.
\]

 \hyperref[prf:identity-domination-laws-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\operatorname{Tautology}(\top)\land \operatorname{Contradiction}(\bot))
\to
(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)\\
&\quad
\left[
(\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot)
\land
(\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\operatorname{Tautology}(\top)\land \operatorname{Contradiction}(\bot))
\to
(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)\\
&\quad
\left[
(\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot)
\land
(\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text: Tautologies act like true constants; contradictions act like false constants.

\]

\[
\varphi\to\psi
\equiv

nodes.name: Biconditional Equivalence Laws
nodes.question: State the theorem: Biconditional Equivalence Laws.
nodes.statement_display:
For all \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\),
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi),
\]
and
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
For all \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\),
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi),
\]
and
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]

 \hyperref[prf:biconditional-equivalence-laws-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.proposition:
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi)
\]
and also
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]
The biconditional says that the two formulas have the same truth value.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{gathered}
(\forall\varphi,\psi\in\WFF)
\left[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi)
\right],\\
(\forall\varphi,\psi\in\WFF)
\left[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi)
\right].
\end{gathered}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{gathered}
(\forall\varphi,\psi\in\WFF)
\left[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi)
\right],\\
(\forall\varphi,\psi\in\WFF)
\left[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi)
\right].
\end{gathered}
\]
nodes.source_text: A biconditional says that two formulas have the same truth value: both true or both false.

nodes.name: Formula Context
nodes.question: State the definition: Formula Context.
nodes.statement_display: A formula context \(C[-]\) is a well-formed formula with one distinguished placeholder occurrence \([-]\). For each well-formed formula \(\varphi\), the expression \(C[\varphi]\) denotes the formula obtained by replacing the placeholder with \(\varphi\).
nodes.statement_tex: A formula context \(C[-]\) is a well-formed formula with one distinguished placeholder occurrence \([-]\). For each well-formed formula \(\varphi\), the expression \(C[\varphi]\) denotes the formula obtained by replacing the placeholder with \(\varphi\).
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{FormulaContext}(C[-])
\]
means that \(C[-]\) is a one-hole propositional formula context.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{FormulaContext}(C[-])
\Longrightarrow
(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)(C[\varphi]\in\WFF).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{FormulaContext}(C[-])
\Longrightarrow
(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)(C[\varphi]\in\WFF).
\]
nodes.source_text: A formula context is a syntactic environment into which a formula can be inserted. Contexts make precise the idea of replacing a subformula inside a larger formula.

\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\Longrightarrow
C[\varphi]\equiv C[\psi].
\]

\]

nodes.name: Argument Form
nodes.question: State the definition: Argument Form.
nodes.statement_display:
An \emph{argument form} is a schematic pattern consisting of a finite list of
premise formulas and one conclusion formula.
nodes.statement_tex:
An \emph{argument form} is a schematic pattern consisting of a finite list of
premise formulas and one conclusion formula.
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{ArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)\) means that \(\Gamma\) is the set
or finite list of premises and \(\varphi\) is the conclusion.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{ArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\text{ is finite and }\varphi\in\WFF.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{ArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\text{ is finite and }\varphi\in\WFF.
\]
nodes.source_text:
An argument form records a pattern of inference independently of the particular
subject matter. Its validity depends on truth preservation, not on whether the
individual formulas happen to be true in one example.

nodes.name: Valid Argument Form
nodes.question: State the definition: Valid Argument Form.
nodes.statement_display:
An argument form with premises \(\Gamma\) and conclusion \(\varphi\) is
\emph{valid} if every truth assignment that satisfies every formula in
\(\Gamma\) also satisfies \(\varphi\).
nodes.statement_tex:
An argument form with premises \(\Gamma\) and conclusion \(\varphi\) is
\emph{valid} if every truth assignment that satisfies every formula in
\(\Gamma\) also satisfies \(\varphi\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)\) means that truth of all
premises forces truth of the conclusion under every truth assignment.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v)\bigl((\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)
\to v\models\varphi\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v)\bigl((\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)
\to v\models\varphi\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Validity is a preservation property. A valid argument form may have false
premises in a particular instance, but it cannot have true premises and a false
conclusion under the same truth assignment.

Truth-Table Validity Test for Argument Forms

nodes.name: Counterexample Assignment
nodes.question: State the definition: Counterexample Assignment.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{counterexample assignment} to an argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is a
truth assignment that satisfies every premise in \(\Gamma\) and does not satisfy
\(\varphi\).
nodes.statement_tex:
A \emph{counterexample assignment} to an argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is a
truth assignment that satisfies every premise in \(\Gamma\) and does not satisfy
\(\varphi\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi)\) means that \(v\)
shows the premises can all be true while the conclusion is false.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)\land v\not\models\varphi.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)\land v\not\models\varphi.
\]
nodes.source_text:
A counterexample assignment is the semantic witness to invalidity. Finding one
settles the question: the argument form is not truth-preserving.

nodes.name: Truth-Table Validity Test for Argument Forms
nodes.question: State the theorem: Truth-Table Validity Test for Argument Forms.
nodes.statement_display:
An argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is valid if and only if no row of its truth
table makes every formula in \(\Gamma\) true and \(\varphi\) false.
nodes.proposition:
The argument form is valid exactly when there is no counterexample truth
assignment.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\neg(\exists v)\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\neg(\exists v)\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi).
\]
nodes.source_text:
The truth-table test is finite because only the variables appearing in the
premises and conclusion matter. A failed row is a counterexample assignment; the
absence of such rows proves semantic validity.

nodes.name: Informal Proof Pattern
nodes.question: State the definition: Informal Proof Pattern.
nodes.statement_display:
An \emph{informal proof pattern} is a reusable truth-preserving strategy for
organizing an ordinary mathematical proof.
nodes.statement_tex:
An \emph{informal proof pattern} is a reusable truth-preserving strategy for
organizing an ordinary mathematical proof.
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{InformalProofPattern}(\Pi)\) means that \(\Pi\) is a recognized
proof strategy whose correctness rests on truth-preserving inference.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{InformalProofPattern}(\Pi)
\Longrightarrow
\Pi\text{ is justified by one or more valid argument forms.}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{InformalProofPattern}(\Pi)
\Longrightarrow
\Pi\text{ is justified by one or more valid argument forms.}
\]
nodes.source_text:
Informal proof patterns are not a substitute for proof. They are templates for
arranging valid moves so that a proof has a clear logical shape.

nodes.name: Affirming the Consequent is Invalid
nodes.question: State the theorem: Affirming the Consequent is Invalid.
nodes.statement_display:
The argument form
\[
\varphi\to\psi,\qquad \psi \quad\therefore\quad \varphi
\]
is invalid.
nodes.statement_tex:
The argument form
\[
\varphi\to\psi,\qquad \psi \quad\therefore\quad \varphi
\]
is invalid.

 \hyperref[prf:affirming-consequent-invalid-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.proposition:
There is a truth assignment under which \(\varphi\to\psi\) and \(\psi\) are true
while \(\varphi\) is false.
nodes.formal:
\[
\neg\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\{\varphi\to\psi,\psi\},\varphi).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\neg\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\{\varphi\to\psi,\psi\},\varphi).
\]
nodes.source_text:
A conditional can be true because both antecedent and consequent are true, but
also because the antecedent is false. Therefore truth of the consequent does not
force truth of the antecedent.

nodes.name: Rule of Replacement
nodes.question: State the definition: Rule of Replacement.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{rule of replacement} is a schematic permission to replace a subformula
by a logically equivalent formula inside a formula context.
nodes.statement_tex:
A \emph{rule of replacement} is a schematic permission to replace a subformula
by a logically equivalent formula inside a formula context.
nodes.proposition:
A rule of replacement licenses an equivalence-preserving rewrite inside a larger
formula.
nodes.formal:
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\Longrightarrow
C[\varphi]\equiv C[\psi].
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\Longrightarrow
C[\varphi]\equiv C[\psi].
\]
nodes.source_text:
Rules of replacement differ from rules of inference. Inference rules move from
premises to conclusions; replacement rules rewrite formulas without changing
truth behavior.

nodes.name: Replacement Rules Preserve Logical Equivalence
nodes.question: State the theorem: Replacement Rules Preserve Logical Equivalence.
nodes.statement_display:
If a formula \(\psi\) is obtained from a formula \(\varphi\) by finitely many
applications of rules of replacement, then \(\varphi\equiv\psi\).
nodes.proposition:
A finite sequence of equivalence-preserving replacements preserves logical
equivalence from the first formula to the last formula.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{ReplacementSequence}(\varphi,\psi)
\Longrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\psi.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{ReplacementSequence}(\varphi,\psi)
\Longrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\psi.
\]
nodes.source_text:
Replacement rules justify algebraic manipulation of formulas. Each local rewrite
preserves truth under every truth assignment, so the entire finite rewrite chain
also preserves truth under every truth assignment.
depends_on_titles: Logical Equivalence is an Equivalence Relation

nodes.name: Tautological Implication Gives a Valid Argument Form
nodes.question: State the theorem: Tautological Implication Gives a Valid Argument Form.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\Gamma=\{\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n\}\subseteq\WFF\) and let
\(\varphi\in\WFF\). If
\[
(\gamma_1\land\cdots\land\gamma_n)\to\varphi
\]
is a tautology, then the argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is valid.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\Gamma=\{\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n\}\subseteq\WFF\) and let
\(\varphi\in\WFF\). If
\[
(\gamma_1\land\cdots\land\gamma_n)\to\varphi
\]
is a tautology, then the argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is valid.

 \hyperref[prf:tautological-implication-valid-argument-form-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.proposition:
If the conditional from the conjunction of all premises to the conclusion is
always true, then the premises cannot all be true while the conclusion is false.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Tautology}((\gamma_1\land\cdots\land\gamma_n)\to\varphi)
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\{\gamma_1,
\ldots,\gamma_n\},\varphi).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{Tautology}((\gamma_1\land\cdots\land\gamma_n)\to\varphi)
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\{\gamma_1,
\ldots,\gamma_n\},\varphi).
\]
nodes.source_text:
This theorem converts a tautology check into an argument-validity check. It is
one reason truth tables can validate named inference rules.

 \hyperref[prf:constructive-dilemma-validity-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.proposition:
If one of two antecedents holds, and each antecedent has its own consequence,
then at least one corresponding consequence holds.
nodes.formal:

nodes.statement_display:

satisfiable, then \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable.

truth assignment for all of \(\Gamma\).

\Rightarrow
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma).

\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)

\Rightarrow

\]
Compactness says that unsatisfiability cannot first appear only at the infinite
level.

truth assignment. Equivalently, every propositional inconsistency has a finite
witness.

nodes.name: Satisfiable Set of Propositional Formulas
nodes.question: State the definition: Satisfiable Set of Propositional Formulas.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\). The set \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable if there exists a
truth assignment \(v\) such that \(v\models\Gamma\).
\[
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land v\models\Gamma\bigr).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\). The set \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable if there exists a
truth assignment \(v\) such that \(v\models\Gamma\).
\[
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land v\models\Gamma\bigr).
\]
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\]
means that one truth assignment makes every formula in \(\Gamma\) true.
nodes.formal:
\[
\Gamma\text{ is satisfiable}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land
\forall\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{True})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\Gamma\text{ is satisfiable}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land
\forall\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{True})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\Rightarrow
\exists\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{False})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\Rightarrow
\exists\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{False})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_predicate:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\]
means that every truth assignment fails on at least one formula in \(\Gamma\).
nodes.failure_modes:
Satisfiability fails when every truth assignment is blocked by at least one
formula in \(\Gamma\).
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\Rightarrow
\exists\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{False})\Bigr).
\]
Thus \(\Gamma\) is not satisfiable exactly when every truth assignment is
defeated by at least one formula from \(\Gamma\).
nodes.source_text:
Satisfiability of a set is a compatibility condition. The formulas in
\(\Gamma\) may impose many requirements, but they are satisfiable only if all
of those requirements can be met by the same truth assignment.

nodes.name: Representation of a Boolean Function
nodes.question: State the definition: Representation of a Boolean Function.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) be a Boolean function. A formula
\(\varphi\in\WFF\) with variables among \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) \emph{represents}
\(f\) if for every truth assignment \(v\),
\[
\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n)).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

\(\varphi\in\WFF\) with variables among \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) \emph{represents}
\(f\) if for every truth assignment \(v\),
\[
\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n)).
\]
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)\) means that
\(\varphi\) has exactly the same truth table as the Boolean function \(f\) on
the listed variables.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B})
\bigl(\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n))\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B})
\bigl(\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n))\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
A formula represents a Boolean function when the formula computes the same
truth value as the function for every input row. This turns a semantic table of
values into a syntactic object inside the propositional language.

nodes.name: DNF Representation of Boolean Functions
nodes.question: State the theorem: DNF Representation of Boolean Functions.
nodes.statement_display:
Every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) is represented by a
formula in disjunctive normal form using variables \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\).
nodes.proposition:
Every \(n\)-ary Boolean function has a propositional formula representative, and
one may choose the representative to be in disjunctive normal form.
nodes.formal:
\[
(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF)
\bigl(\varphi\text{ is in DNF}\land
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF)
\bigl(\varphi\text{ is in DNF}\land
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
A truth table specifies which input rows make the Boolean function true. For
each true row, form the corresponding conjunction of literals; the disjunction
of those row conjunctions represents the entire function.

nodes.name: Functionally Complete Connective Set
nodes.question: State the definition: Functionally Complete Connective Set.
nodes.statement_display:
A connective basis \(B\) is \emph{functionally complete} if every Boolean
function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\), for every \(n\ge 1\), is represented
by some formula using only connectives from \(B\).
nodes.statement_tex:
A connective basis \(B\) is \emph{functionally complete} if every Boolean
function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\), for every \(n\ge 1\), is represented
by some formula using only connectives from \(B\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)\) means that formulas over \(B\) can
represent every finite Boolean input-output table.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall n\ge 1)(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF_B)
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall n\ge 1)(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF_B)
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Functional completeness is the central expressive-power property for connective
sets. It says that the basis can express all possible truth-functional behavior,
not merely the connectives originally listed in the language.

nodes.name: Expressively Equivalent Connective Sets
nodes.question: State the definition: Expressively Equivalent Connective Sets.
nodes.statement_display:
Two connective bases \(B\) and \(C\) are \emph{expressively equivalent} if every
connective in \(B\) is definable from \(C\), and every connective in \(C\) is
definable from \(B\).
nodes.statement_tex:
Two connective bases \(B\) and \(C\) are \emph{expressively equivalent} if every
connective in \(B\) is definable from \(C\), and every connective in \(C\) is
definable from \(B\).
nodes.proposition:
\(B\equiv_{\mathrm{expr}} C\) means that the two bases can define exactly the
same connective behavior.
nodes.formal:
\[
B\equiv_{\mathrm{expr}} C
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl((\forall\circ\in B)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\circ,C)\bigr)
\land
\bigl((\forall\star\in C)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\star,B)\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
B\equiv_{\mathrm{expr}} C
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl((\forall\circ\in B)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\circ,C)\bigr)
\land
\bigl((\forall\star\in C)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\star,B)\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Expressive equivalence lets a proof replace one primitive vocabulary with
another. This is why a language can be simplified syntactically without changing
which truth functions can be expressed.

nodes.name: Monotone Boolean Function
nodes.question: State the definition: Monotone Boolean Function.
nodes.statement_display:
A Boolean function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) is \emph{monotone} if
changing input coordinates from \(\False\) to \(\True\) never changes the output
from \(\True\) to \(\False\).
nodes.statement_tex:
A Boolean function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) is \emph{monotone} if
changing input coordinates from \(\False\) to \(\True\) never changes the output
from \(\True\) to \(\False\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{Monotone}(f)\) means that increasing truth inputs cannot make the
output decrease from true to false.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Monotone}(f)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall a,b\in\mathbb{B}^n)
\bigl(a\le b\to f(a)\le f(b)\bigr),
\]
where \(\False\le\True\) coordinatewise.
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{Monotone}(f)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall a,b\in\mathbb{B}^n)
\bigl(a\le b\to f(a)\le f(b)\bigr),
\]
where \(\False\le\True\) coordinatewise.
nodes.source_text:
The connectives \(\land\) and \(\lor\) are monotone. Negation is not monotone,
because changing \(P\) from false to true changes \(\neg P\) from true to false.

nodes.source_text:
NOR can define negation and disjunction:
\[
\neg\varphi\equiv\varphi\downarrow\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\psi\equiv(\varphi\downarrow\psi)\downarrow(\varphi\downarrow\psi).
\]
Once negation and disjunction are definable, functional completeness follows
from the functional completeness of \(\{\neg,\lor\}\).

nodes.name: Connective Reduction
nodes.question: State the definition: Connective Reduction.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{connective reduction} replaces a formula using one connective basis by
a logically equivalent formula using a smaller or different connective basis.
nodes.statement_tex:
A \emph{connective reduction} replaces a formula using one connective basis by
a logically equivalent formula using a smaller or different connective basis.
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{Reduction}_{B\to C}(\varphi,\psi)\) means that \(\psi\) is a
translation of \(\varphi\) into the connective basis \(C\) without changing truth
behavior.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Reduction}_{B\to C}(\varphi,\psi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\psi
\quad\text{and}\quad
\psi\in\WFF_C.
\]

\[

\Longleftrightarrow

\quad\text{and}\quad

\]
nodes.source_text:
Reduction shows that some primitive connectives are optional. If a connective is
definable from the remaining basis, then formulas using that connective can be
translated away.

nodes.name: Negation and Conjunction are Functionally Complete
nodes.question: State the theorem: Negation and Conjunction are Functionally Complete.
nodes.statement_display:
The connective basis
\[
\{\neg,\land\}
\]
is functionally complete.
nodes.proposition:
Every Boolean function is represented by a formula using only negation and
conjunction.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(\{\neg,\land\}).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(\{\neg,\land\}).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Disjunction is definable from negation and conjunction by De Morgan's law:
\[
\varphi\lor\psi\equiv\neg(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]
Thus every formula using \(\neg,\land,\lor\) can be translated into an equivalent
formula using only \(\neg\) and \(\land\).

nodes.name: Canonical Disjunctive Normal Form
nodes.question: State the definition: Canonical Disjunctive Normal Form.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\), and fix an ordering \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) of the finite
variable set of \(\varphi\). The \emph{canonical disjunctive normal form} of
\(\varphi\) relative to this ordering is the disjunction of the

corresponding to the rows on which \(\varphi\) is true.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\), and fix an ordering \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) of the finite
variable set of \(\varphi\). The \emph{canonical disjunctive normal form} of
\(\varphi\) relative to this ordering is the disjunction of the

corresponding to the rows on which \(\varphi\) is true.
nodes.formal:
For \(\mathrm{Var}(\varphi)=\{P_1,\ldots,P_n\}\), the canonical
disjunctive normal form is
\[
\bigvee_{\widehat v(\varphi)=\True}
\bigl(L_1\land\cdots\land L_n\bigr),
\]
where each row conjunction is determined by the truth-table row of \(v\).
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
For \(\mathrm{Var}(\varphi)=\{P_1,\ldots,P_n\}\), the canonical
disjunctive normal form is
\[
\bigvee_{\widehat v(\varphi)=\True}
\bigl(L_1\land\cdots\land L_n\bigr),
\]
where each row conjunction is determined by the truth-table row of \(v\).
nodes.source_text:
Canonical DNF records exactly the truth-table rows on which the formula is
true, using one row conjunction for each true row.

nodes.name: Elementary Disjunction
nodes.question: State the definition: Elementary Disjunction.
nodes.statement_display:
An \emph{elementary disjunction} is a finite disjunction of
\hyperref[def:literal-propositional-logic]{literals}. That is, it is a
\hyperref[def:clause-propositional-logic]{clause} of the form
\[
L_1\lor L_2\lor\cdots\lor L_k,
\]
where each \(L_i\) is a literal. The one-literal case is permitted.
nodes.statement_tex:
An \emph{elementary disjunction} is a finite disjunction of
\hyperref[def:literal-propositional-logic]{literals}. That is, it is a
\hyperref[def:clause-propositional-logic]{clause} of the form
\[
L_1\lor L_2\lor\cdots\lor L_k,
\]
where each \(L_i\) is a literal. The one-literal case is permitted.
nodes.formal:
\[
L_1\lor L_2\lor\cdots\lor L_k,
\qquad
L_i\text{ is a literal for each }i.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
L_1\lor L_2\lor\cdots\lor L_k,
\qquad
L_i\text{ is a literal for each }i.
\]
nodes.source_text:
Elementary disjunctions are the clause-level building blocks used in
conjunctive normal form. They record finite literal alternatives.

nodes.name: Conjunctive Normal Form
nodes.question: State the definition: Conjunctive Normal Form.
nodes.statement_display:
A formula is in \emph{conjunctive normal form}, abbreviated \emph{CNF}, when it
is a finite conjunction of
\hyperref[def:clause-propositional-logic]{clauses}. Equivalently, it has the
shape
\[
C_1\land C_2\land\cdots\land C_m,
\]
where each \(C_j\) is a clause.
nodes.statement_tex:
A formula is in \emph{conjunctive normal form}, abbreviated \emph{CNF}, when it
is a finite conjunction of
\hyperref[def:clause-propositional-logic]{clauses}. Equivalently, it has the
shape
\[
C_1\land C_2\land\cdots\land C_m,
\]
where each \(C_j\) is a clause.
nodes.formal:
\[
\varphi\text{ is in CNF}
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi=C_1\land C_2\land\cdots\land C_m
\]
for finitely many clauses \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\).
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\varphi\text{ is in CNF}
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi=C_1\land C_2\land\cdots\land C_m
\]
for finitely many clauses \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\).
nodes.source_text:
CNF is a syntactic form used to expose clause-by-clause constraints. Replacing
a formula by a
\hyperref[def:logical-equivalence-propositional-logic]{logically equivalent}
CNF formula turns global validity and
\hyperref[def:contradiction-propositional-logic]{contradiction} questions into
questions about the interaction of its clauses.

nodes.name: Disjunctive Normal Form

C_1\lor C_2\lor\cdots\lor C_m,
\]
where each \(C_j\) is an elementary conjunction.

\hyperref[def:elementary-conjunction-propositional-logic]{elementary conjunctions}.

\[
C_1\lor C_2\lor\cdots\lor C_m,
\]
where each \(C_j\) is an elementary conjunction.

\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi=C_1\lor C_2\lor\cdots\lor C_m

\[

nodes.question: State the definition: NNF Conversion Procedure.
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{NNFConversionProcedure}(\varphi,\psi)
\]
means that \(\psi\) is obtained from \(\varphi\) by eliminating
biconditionals and conditionals, removing double negations, and pushing
remaining negations inward.
nodes.formal:
Starting with \(\varphi\in\WFF\), repeatedly apply the equivalences
\[
\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta
\equiv
(\alpha\to\beta)\land(\beta\to\alpha),
\qquad
\alpha\to\beta\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\beta,
\]
\[
\neg\neg\alpha\equiv\alpha,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\land\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\neg\beta,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\lor\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\land\neg\beta,
\]
until negations occur only immediately before propositional variables and only
\(\land\) and \(\lor\) remain above the literal level.
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
Starting with \(\varphi\in\WFF\), repeatedly apply the equivalences
\[
\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta
\equiv
(\alpha\to\beta)\land(\beta\to\alpha),
\qquad
\alpha\to\beta\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\beta,
\]
\[
\neg\neg\alpha\equiv\alpha,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\land\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\neg\beta,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\lor\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\land\neg\beta,
\]
until negations occur only immediately before propositional variables and only
\(\land\) and \(\lor\) remain above the literal level.
nodes.source_text:
The procedure is a syntax-directed rewrite process. Each rewrite step is backed
by a logical equivalence law, so the output formula has the same truth
conditions as the input formula.

nodes.statement_display:

\[

\[

\]
defined recursively as follows:
\[
\widehat v(P)=v(P)
\quad\text{for every }P\in\Prop,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\neg\varphi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\False,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\land\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ and }
\widehat v(\psi)=\True,
\]
\[

\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ or }
\widehat v(\psi)=\True,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\to\psi)=\False
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ and }
\widehat v(\psi)=\False,
\]
and
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\widehat v(\psi).
\]

Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\) and suppose the variables occurring in \(\varphi\) are among \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\). A truth table for \(\varphi\) is a finite table with one row for each assignment

nodes.name: Logical Connective
nodes.question: State the definition: Logical Connective.
nodes.statement_display:
The standard primitive propositional connectives are
\[
\neg,\qquad \land,\qquad \lor,\qquad \to,\qquad \leftrightarrow.
\]
The connective \(\neg\) is unary. The connectives \(\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\) are binary.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{Symbol} & \text{Name} & \text{Arity} & \text{Formation pattern} & \text{Reading}\\
\hline
\neg & \text{negation} & \text{unary} & \neg\varphi & \text{not }\varphi\\
\land & \text{conjunction} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\land\psi) & \varphi\text{ and }\psi\\
\lor & \text{disjunction} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\lor\psi) & \varphi\text{ or }\psi\\
\to & \text{conditional} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\to\psi) & \text{if }\varphi,\text{ then }\psi\\
\leftrightarrow & \text{biconditional} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi) & \varphi\text{ iff }\psi
\end{array}
\]

nodes.name: Well-Formed Formula
nodes.question: State the definition: Well-Formed Formula.
nodes.statement_display:
The set \(\WFF\) of well-formed formulas is the smallest set of strings satisfying the following formation rules:
- Every propositional variable \(P\in\Prop\) belongs to \(\WFF\).
- If \(\varphi\in\WFF\), then \(\neg\varphi\in\WFF\).
- If \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\) and \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in\WFF\).
- No string is a well-formed formula unless it is obtained by finitely many applications of the previous clauses.
nodes.statement_tex:
The set \(\WFF\) of well-formed formulas is the smallest set of strings satisfying the following formation rules:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every propositional variable \(P\in\Prop\) belongs to \(\WFF\).
\item If \(\varphi\in\WFF\), then \(\neg\varphi\in\WFF\).
\item If \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\) and \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in\WFF\).
\item No string is a well-formed formula unless it is obtained by finitely many applications of the previous clauses.
\end{enumerate}

\right\}.
\]

\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\},

nodes.name: Minimality of Well-Formed Formulas
nodes.question: State the theorem: Minimality of Well-Formed Formulas.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(S\) be a set of strings over the propositional alphabet. Suppose:
- \(\Prop\subseteq S\);
- if \(\varphi\in S\), then \(\neg\varphi\in S\);
- if \(\varphi,\psi\in S\) and
 \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then
 \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in S\).
Then
\[
\WFF\subseteq S.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\forall S)\Big[
&\Prop\subseteq S
\land
(\forall\varphi\in S)(\neg\varphi\in S)\\
&\land
(\forall\varphi,\psi\in S)
(\forall\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\})
((\varphi\circ\psi)\in S)
\Big]
\to
\WFF\subseteq S.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\forall S)\Big[
&\Prop\subseteq S
\land
(\forall\varphi\in S)(\neg\varphi\in S)\\
&\land
(\forall\varphi,\psi\in S)
(\forall\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\})
((\varphi\circ\psi)\in S)
\Big]
\to
\WFF\subseteq S.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
We prove by structural induction on \(\varphi\in\WFF\) that
\(\varphi\in S\).

If \(\varphi\) is atomic, then \(\varphi=P\) for some
\(P\in\Prop\). Since \(\Prop\subseteq S\), it follows that
\(\varphi=P\in S\).

Suppose \(\varphi=\neg\theta\), where \(\theta\in\WFF\). By the induction
hypothesis, \(\theta\in S\). By the second hypothesis on \(S\),
\(\neg\theta\in S\). Hence \(\varphi\in S\).

Suppose \(\varphi=(\theta\circ\psi)\), where
\(\theta,\psi\in\WFF\) and
\[
\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}.
\]
By the induction hypothesis, \(\theta\in S\) and \(\psi\in S\). By the
third hypothesis on \(S\), \((\theta\circ\psi)\in S\). Hence
\(\varphi\in S\).

Therefore every \(\varphi\in\WFF\) belongs to \(S\), and so
\[
\WFF\subseteq S.
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is structural induction following the grammar for \(\WFF\). The
base case uses \(\Prop\subseteq S\). The induction steps use the two closure
assumptions on \(S\).
nodes.source_text:
Minimality is the formal content of the clause ``nothing else is a wff.'' It says

propositional variables and is closed under the formation rules.

nodes.name: Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ is called a \emph{Peano system} exactly when $P$ is a set,
$1 \in P$, $S : P \to P$ is a function, and the following axioms hold:
- $1 \in P$.
- For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
- For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
- For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
- If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
 \[
 \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
 \]
 then $A=P$.
nodes.statement_tex:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ is called a \emph{Peano system} exactly when $P$ is a set,
$1 \in P$, $S : P \to P$ is a function, and the following axioms hold:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[\textbf{P1.}] $1 \in P$.
 \item[\textbf{P2.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
 \item[\textbf{P3.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
 \item[\textbf{P4.}] For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
 \item[\textbf{P5.}] If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
 \[
 \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
 \]
 then $A=P$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P \land S : P \to P \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \neq 1) \\
&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P \land S : P \to P \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \neq 1) \\
&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ fails to be a Peano system if the distinguished element
does not lie in the underlying set, if the successor map leaves the set, if
the successor hits $1$, if the successor identifies two distinct elements, or
if there exists a proper subset of $P$ that contains $1$ and is closed under
successor.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\neg\,\text{$(P,S,1)$ is a Peano system}
\Longrightarrow\;&
1 \notin P \\
&\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n) \notin P) \\
&\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n)=1) \\
&\lor \exists m,n \in P\;(m \neq n \land S(m)=S(n)) \\
&\lor \exists A \subseteq P\;
\bigl(1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A)
\land A \neq P\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
A Peano system is the abstract data of counting: an underlying set, a first
element, and a successor operation satisfying the usual non-collision and
induction principles. The purpose of the definition is to isolate the ambient
object before the individual axioms are recorded and used one by one.

nodes.question: State the corollary: Unique Predecessor Characterization Away from $1$.
nodes.statement_display:

only if there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\forall x \in P\;\bigl(x\neq 1 \Longleftrightarrow
\exists! u \in P\;(S(u)=x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\exists x \in P\;\Bigl(
\bigl(x\neq 1 \land
(\forall u \in P\;(S(u)\neq x)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\lor
\exists u,v \in P\;(S(u)=x \land S(v)=x \land u\neq v))\bigr)\\
&\qquad\qquad\lor
\bigl(x=1 \land \exists u \in P\;(S(u)=x \land
\forall v \in P\;(S(v)=x \Longrightarrow v=u))\bigr)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

&\qquad\qquad\qquad\lor
\exists u,v \in P\;(S(u)=x \land S(v)=x \land u\neq v))\bigr)\\
&\qquad\qquad\lor
\bigl(x=1 \land \exists u \in P\;(S(u)=x \land
\forall v \in P\;(S(v)=x \Longrightarrow v=u))\bigr)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
The biconditional can fail in two ways: a non-initial element can fail to have
a unique predecessor, or the distinguished first element can have a unique
predecessor.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\exists x \in P\;\Bigl(
\underbrace{\bigl(x\neq 1 \land
(\forall u \in P\;(S(u)\neq x)
\lor
\exists u,v \in P\;(S(u)=x \land S(v)=x \land u\neq v))\bigr)}_
{\text{non-initial element lacks a unique predecessor}}\\
&\qquad\qquad\lor
\underbrace{\bigl(x=1 \land \exists u \in P\;(S(u)=x \land
\forall v \in P\;(S(v)=x \Longrightarrow v=u))\bigr)}_
{\text{the first element has a unique predecessor}}
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

having a unique predecessor. This turns the informal phrase "away from $1$"
into an internal characterization of the successor structure.

nodes.question: State the definition: Presburger Signature.
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{Presburger signature} is the first-order signature
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pres}} = \{0, S, +, <, =\},
\]
where $0$ is a constant symbol, $S$ is a unary function symbol, $+$ is a
binary function symbol, and $<$ and $=$ are binary relation symbols.

The Presburger signature names addition and order, but it deliberately omits
multiplication as a function symbol. This makes Presburger arithmetic a theory
of the additive structure of the natural numbers rather than a theory of full
arithmetic.

nodes.name: Presburger Arithmetic
nodes.question: State the definition: Presburger Arithmetic.
nodes.statement_display:
\emph{Presburger arithmetic} is the first-order theory of the natural numbers
in the Presburger signature. Its intended structure is
\[
(\mathbb{N},0,S,+,<,=),
\]
and its axioms describe the behavior of zero, successor, addition, order, and
induction for formulas written in the language
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pres}}$.

\[
\operatorname{PresburgerArithmetic}(T)
\Longleftrightarrow
T \subseteq \operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pres}})
\land T \text{ axiomatizes } (\mathbb{N},0,S,+,<,=).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

\Longleftrightarrow

\]
nodes.source_text:
Presburger arithmetic isolates the part of arithmetic governed by addition.
It is strong enough to express linear equations, congruences, and order
properties of natural numbers, but it cannot directly express multiplication
as a primitive operation. The later Peano-system material supplies the more
general recursive framework from which addition, multiplication, order, and
induction are developed structurally.

nodes.name: Iterator Relation
nodes.question: State the definition: Iterator Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. A
relation $R\subseteq P\times W$ is called an \emph{iterator relation} for
$(W,c,g)$ exactly when
\[
(1,c)\in R
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;\forall w\in W\;
\bigl((n,w)\in R\Longrightarrow (S(n),g(w))\in R\bigr).
\]

nodes.name: Minimal Iterator Relation

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.

\[
R^*
=
\bigcap\{R\subseteq P\times W : R \text{ is an iterator relation for }
(W,c,g)\}.
\]

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. If $(n,w_0)\in R^*$ and
$(n,w_1)\in R^*$, then $w_0=w_1$.

determinacy step in the minimal-relation construction used to turn recursive
specifications into functions \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions
nodes.question: State the lemma: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. If
$f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.

\qquad\text{and}\qquad

\Longrightarrow f=h\Bigr).

\]

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations
nodes.question: State the corollary: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
\[
F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]
and
\[
F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
\[
F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]
and
\[
F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.
nodes.proposition:
For each $a\in A$, write $F_a(n)=F(a,n)$ and $G_a(n)=G(a,n)$. Then
\[
\forall a\in A\;
\bigl(\operatorname{IteratorFunction}(F_a,(P,S,1),W,c_a,g_a)
\land \operatorname{IteratorFunction}(G_a,(P,S,1),W,c_a,g_a)
\Longrightarrow F_a=G_a\bigr).
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\forall a\in A\;\forall n\in P\;&\Bigl(
F(a,1)=c_a\land G(a,1)=c_a\\
&\land F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n))
\land G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow F=G.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[

F(a,1)=c_a\land G(a,1)=c_a\\
&\land F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n))
\land G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow F=G.

nodes.statement_display:

f(1)=c

\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n))).
\]

nodes.question: State the theorem: Uniqueness of Peano Systems up to Isomorphism.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S_P,1_P)$ and $(Q,S_Q,1_Q)$ be Peano systems. Then there exists a
unique bijection $\theta:P\to Q$ such that
\[
\theta(1_P)=1_Q
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(\theta(S_P(n))=S_Q(\theta(n))).
\]
Thus any two Peano systems are isomorphic.

nodes.name: Addition Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Addition Is Well-Defined on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m+n \coloneqq f_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

nodes.source_text:
The theorem shows that the recursive clauses for addition determine exactly one
right-input map for each fixed left input. The addition operation is therefore
not assumed; it is constructed from the successor map by recursion.

nodes.name: $ $ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
- \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
- \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
 \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
 \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
 \item \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
 \item \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
This theorem is a packaging result. It names the algebraic structure that
has been proved piece by piece: the three individual theorems on associativity,
commutativity, and cancellation together certify that $(P,+)$ is a cancellative
commutative semigroup. There is no additive identity in $P$ because $P$ has
no element $0$ with $0+n=n$ for all $n$; the smallest element under addition
is $1$, not an identity.

nodes.name: $ $ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
 $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
- \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
 $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
 \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
 \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
 $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
 \item \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
 $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.
nodes.source_text:
The distinguished first element $1$ is a multiplicative identity on both
sides, so multiplication promotes $P$ from a semigroup to a monoid. The
absence of multiplicative inverses (other than $1^{-1} = 1$, which does not
lie in $P$ in the usual sense) is what prevents $(P,\cdot)$ from being a
group. The structural limitation is intrinsic: no element of $P$ other than
$1$ has a reciprocal in $P$.

nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is a Semiring.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Then $(P,+,\cdot)$ satisfies:
- $(P,+)$ is a commutative semigroup.
- $(P,\cdot,1)$ is a commutative monoid.
- Multiplication distributes over addition: for all $a,b,c \in P$,
 \[
 a \cdot (b+c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c).
 \]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Then $(P,+,\cdot)$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item $(P,+)$ is a commutative semigroup.
 \item $(P,\cdot,1)$ is a commutative monoid.
 \item Multiplication distributes over addition: for all $a,b,c \in P$,
 \[
 a \cdot (b+c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c).
 \]
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
A semiring packages the interaction of two operations without requiring
additive inverses. The natural numbers are the canonical example of a semiring
that is not a ring: they satisfy every ring axiom except the existence of
additive inverses, which fails because there is no element $-1$ in $P$.
The integers are the smallest ring extending $P$ that repairs this failure.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Multiplication Is Well-Defined on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
g_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
g_m(1)=m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(g_m(S(n))=g_m(n)+m).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m \cdot n \coloneqq g_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

adding copies of $a$, so a sum in the second factor splits into two separate
blocks of repeated addition. This is the bridge between the additive and
multiplicative structures.

nodes.name: Left Distributivity of Multiplication Over Addition
nodes.question: State the theorem: Left Distributivity of Multiplication Over Addition.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
(a+b)\cdot c=(a\cdot c)+(b\cdot c).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
(a+b)\cdot c=(a\cdot c)+(b\cdot c).
\]
nodes.source_text:
The existing distributive law expands a sum in the right factor. This theorem
expands a sum in the left factor. It follows from right distributivity together
with commutativity of multiplication.

nodes.name: Multiplication Is Associative
nodes.question: State the theorem: Multiplication Is Associative.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

\]
nodes.source_text:
Associativity shows that repeated multiplication can be regrouped without
changing the value. Once this law is established, longer products can be used
without parenthetical ambiguity.

nodes.statement_display:

a \cdot b = b \cdot a.

nodes.statement_tex:

nodes.source_text:

operation is symmetric in the two factors. Commutativity shows that repeated
addition of $a$ to build $a \cdot b$ agrees exactly with repeated addition of
$b$ to build $b \cdot a$.

nodes.name: The Natural Numbers
nodes.question: State the definition: The Natural Numbers.
nodes.statement_display:
The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ are the canonical Peano system
\[
(\mathbb{N},1,S),
\]
where $1 \in \mathbb{N}$ is the distinguished base element and
$S:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is the successor operation.

nodes.name: Strict Less Than on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Strict Less Than on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[
a<b
\]
exactly when there exists $c \in P$ such that
\[
b=a+c.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[
a<b
\]
exactly when there exists $c \in P$ such that
\[
b=a+c.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists c \in P\;(b=a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists c \in P\;(b=a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
Strict inequality fails exactly when no additive witness in $P$ carries $a$ to
$b$. In that case, every nontrivial additive step from $a$ misses $b$.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\underbrace{\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c)}_{\text{every proposed additive witness fails}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
The strict order records whether $b$ lies genuinely ahead of $a$ in the
counting structure. The witness $c$ is the amount of additive displacement
needed to move from $a$ to $b$.

nodes.name: Less Than or Equal on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Less Than or Equal on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[
a \le b
\]
exactly when
\[
a<b
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
a=b.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[
a \le b
\]
exactly when
\[
a<b
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
a=b.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \le b
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(a<b \lor a=b\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \le b
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(a<b \lor a=b\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not\le b
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(a \not< b \land a \neq b\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not\le b
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(a \not< b \land a \neq b\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
The non-strict order fails in exactly two simultaneous ways: $a$ is not
strictly below $b$, and $a$ is not equal to $b$. Thus $b$ neither lies ahead
of $a$ nor coincides with it.
nodes.source_text:
The relation $a \le b$ allows either equality or a genuine forward step from
$a$ to $b$. It is the additive order relation derived from the strict witness
definition.

nodes.name: Order Is Transitive on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Order Is Transitive on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
\bigl(a \le b \land b \le c\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
a \le c.
\]

\[
\bigl(a \le b \land b \le c\bigr)

\]
nodes.source_text:
If $b$ lies at or beyond $a$, and $c$ lies at or beyond $b$, then $c$ also
lies at or beyond $a$. Transitivity expresses the consistency of additive
comparison along a chain.

nodes.question: State the theorem: $n < 2^n$ for All $n $.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $2 \coloneqq S(1)$. For every $n \in P$,
\[
n < 2^n.
\]

n < 2^n.

nodes.source_text:
The base case $1 < 2 = 2^1$ holds by definition of $2$ and the strict order.
For the inductive step, assume $n < 2^n$. Then $2^{S(n)} = 2^n \cdot 2$.
Since $2^n > n \ge 1$, we have $2^n \cdot 2 > n \cdot 2 = n + n > n + 1 = S(n)$,
where the last step uses that $n \ge 1$ so $n + n > n + 1$. Hence $S(n) < 2^{S(n)}$.
The inequality $n < 2^n$ is the threshold that distinguishes the growth regimes
and reappears in every comparison between polynomial and exponential bounds.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Well-Ordering Principle.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
element with respect to the order $\le$ on $P$.
nodes.statement_tex:

nodes.failure_modes:
The well-ordering principle would fail if some nonempty subset of $P$ had no
least element. That means for every candidate minimum, a strictly smaller
element of the subset exists, producing an infinite strictly descending chain
in $P$. Induction rules this out.
nodes.source_text:
The well-ordering principle is the order-theoretic complement to induction.
Induction says one can build up: start at $1$ and keep stepping forward.
Well-ordering says one can always descend to a minimum: any nonempty set has
a floor. Proof strategies that use well-ordering typically assume a property
fails somewhere, form the set of failures, extract its minimum by
well-ordering, and derive a contradiction from the minimality of that element.

nodes.name: Induction, Strong Induction, and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent
nodes.question: State the theorem: Induction, Strong Induction, and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
- The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
 $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
 for all $n \in P$.
- The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
 if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
 $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
- The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
 element with respect to $\le$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
 $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
 for all $n \in P$.
 \item The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
 if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
 $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
 \item The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
 element with respect to $\le$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
Induction proves well-ordering by contrapositive: if a nonempty set $A$ had
no least element, the set of non-members of $A$ would be inductive, forcing
$A = \varnothing$, a contradiction. Well-ordering proves induction by forming
the set of elements where $\varphi$ fails and, if nonempty, extracting a
least failure to derive a contradiction with the successor step.

nodes.question: State the proposition: Uniqueness of the Maximum.

nodes.name: Maximum Implies Supremum
nodes.question: State the proposition: Maximum Implies Supremum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $m\in A$. If $m$ is a maximum of $A$, then $m=\sup A$.

\[

&m\text{ is a maximum of }A
\Longrightarrow
m=\sup A.

\]

\[

&m\text{ is a maximum of }A
\Longrightarrow

\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ and }m\in A.\\
&m\text{ is a maximum of }A
\text{ and }m\ne\sup A

\]

nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ and }m\in A.\\
&m\text{ is a maximum of }A
\text{ and }m\ne\sup A
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.failure_modes: The implication could fail only if the greatest element of $A$ were not the least upper bound of $A$. But a maximum already bounds the set from above, and every upper bound must lie at least as high as that maximum.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Maximum}(m,A)
&\Longrightarrow
\underbrace{\forall x\in A\;(x\le m)}_{m\text{ is an upper bound}}\\
&\qquad\land
\underbrace{\forall u\in\mathbb{R}\,
\bigl[(\forall x\in A\;(x\le u))\Longrightarrow m\le u\bigr]}_{m\text{ is least among upper bounds}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Suppose \(m\) is a maximum of \(A\). Then \(m\in A\) and
\[
x\le m
\]
for every \(x\in A\). Hence \(m\) is an upper bound of \(A\).

Now let \(u\) be any upper bound of \(A\). Since \(m\in A\), the upper-bound
property of \(u\) gives \(m\le u\). Thus every upper bound \(u\) of \(A\)
satisfies \(m\le u\). Therefore \(m\) is the least upper bound of \(A\), so
\[
m=\sup A.
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
A maximum is already an upper bound because it dominates every element of the
set. It is least among upper bounds because it is itself an element of the set:
any upper bound must bound \(m\) too.
nodes.source_text: A maximum belongs to the set and sits above every element of the set. That makes it an upper bound, and no smaller upper bound can exist because it would have to sit below the maximum while still bounding the maximum itself.

nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Supremum}(s,A)\land s\in A
&\Longrightarrow
\underbrace{\forall x\in A\;(x\le s)}_{s\text{ is an upper bound}}\\
&\qquad\land
\underbrace{s\in A}_{s\text{ belongs to the set}}
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{Maximum}(s,A).
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Subset Inclusion Preserves Upper Bounds
nodes.question: State the lemma: Subset Inclusion Preserves Upper Bounds.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound of $A$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound of $A$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }A\subseteq B\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ and }u\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&\bigl[\forall y\in B\;(y\le u)\bigr]
\Longrightarrow
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le u)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }A\subseteq B\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ and }u\in\mathbb{R}.\\

\Longrightarrow
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le u)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Since \(s=\sup A\), the definition of supremum says, in particular, that
\(s\) is an upper bound of \(A\). Hence every element of \(A\) lies below
\(s\): for every \(x\in A\),
\[
x\le s.
\]
nodes.proof_idea:

upper-bound part of \(s=\sup A\); the minimality of \(s\) among upper bounds is
not needed.

nodes.name: Infimum Is Less Than or Equal to the Supremum
nodes.question: State the theorem: Infimum Is Less Than or Equal to the Supremum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty, bounded below, and bounded above. Then $\inf A\le \sup A$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty, bounded below, and bounded above. Then $\inf A\le \sup A$.
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\inf A>\sup A
\]
is impossible for a nonempty set that has both bounds.
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\inf A>\sup A
\]
is impossible for a nonempty set that has both bounds.
nodes.failure_modes: The inequality could fail only if the greatest lower bound were strictly above the least upper bound. Any element of the nonempty set must lie between those two bounding values, which rules out this order.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Because \(A\) is nonempty, choose \(x\in A\). Since \(\inf A\) is a lower
bound of \(A\), we have
\[
\inf A\le x.
\]
Since \(\sup A\) is an upper bound of \(A\), we have
\[
x\le \sup A.
\]
By transitivity of the order on \(\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\inf A\le \sup A.
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
Choose one element of the nonempty set. The lower-bound part of the infimum
definition places \(\inf A\) below that element, and the upper-bound part of
the supremum definition places the element below \(\sup A\). Transitivity
finishes the comparison.
nodes.source_text: A nonempty bounded set cannot have its floor above its ceiling. Any point of the set witnesses the bridge from the infimum up to the supremum.

nodes.name: Translation Invariance of the Supremum
nodes.question: State the theorem: Translation Invariance of the Supremum.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
\[
 \sup(A+c)=\sup A+c,
 \qquad
 A+c=\{a+c:a\in A\}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
\[
 \sup(A+c)=\sup A+c,
 \qquad
 A+c=\{a+c:a\in A\}.
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\sup(A+c)\ne \sup A+c
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\sup(A+c)\ne \sup A+c
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.
nodes.failure_modes: The formula could fail only if translation either failed to preserve upper bounds or failed to preserve leastness. Adding the same real number to every comparison preserves the order, so neither failure mode can occur.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\forall a\in A\;(a\le s)
&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall a\in A\;(a+c\le s+c),\\
\forall u\,[\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A)\Longrightarrow s\le u]
&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,[\operatorname{UpperBound}(v,A+c)\Longrightarrow s+c\le v].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text: Translation shifts the entire set and all of its ceilings by the same amount. The least ceiling therefore shifts by exactly that amount.

\LRAProofBodyStart
Let \(i=\inf A\). We prove that \(-i\) is the supremum of \(-A\).

First let \(y\in -A\). Then \(y=-x\) for some \(x\in A\). Since \(i\) is a
lower bound of \(A\), we have \(i\le x\). Multiplying by \(-1\) reverses the
inequality, so
\[
y=-x\le -i.
\]
Thus \(-i\) is an upper bound of \(-A\). In particular, \(-A\) is bounded
above.

Now let \(u\) be any upper bound of \(-A\). For every \(x\in A\), the element
\(-x\) belongs to \(-A\), so
\[
-x\le u.
\]
Multiplying by \(-1\) gives
\[
-u\le x
\]
for every \(x\in A\). Hence \(-u\) is a lower bound of \(A\). Since \(i=\inf A\)
is the greatest lower bound of \(A\), we have \(-u\le i\). Multiplying by
\(-1\) again gives
\[
-i\le u.
\]
Therefore every upper bound \(u\) of \(-A\) lies above \(-i\). Since \(-i\) is
itself an upper bound of \(-A\), it is the least upper bound of \(-A\). Hence
\[
\sup(-A)=-i=-\inf A.
\]
nodes.proof_idea:
Negation reverses order. Lower bounds of \(A\) become upper bounds of \(-A\),
and the greatest lower bound becomes the least upper bound after multiplying
all inequalities by \(-1\).
nodes.source_text: Negation reflects the real line through the origin. Floors become ceilings, so the infimum of the original set becomes the negative of the supremum of the reflected set.

\]

\[

 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \sup(A+B)\le \sup A+\sup B.
\]

\]

nodes.statement_display: Let $(S,\le_S)$ and $(T,\le_T)$ be ordered sets, and let $A\subseteq S\cap T$. Whether $u$ is an upper bound of $A$ must be interpreted relative to the chosen ambient order.

\[
\begin{aligned}
&u\text{ is an upper bound of }A\text{ in }S
\Longleftrightarrow
u\in S\text{ and }\forall x\in A\;(x\le_S u),\\
&u\text{ is an upper bound of }A\text{ in }T
\Longleftrightarrow
u\in T\text{ and }\forall x\in A\;(x\le_T u).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[

&u\text{ is an upper bound of }A\text{ in }T
\Longleftrightarrow
u\in T\text{ and }\forall x\in A\;(x\le_T u).
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Epsilon Characterization of Supremum
nodes.question: State the definition: Epsilon Characterization of Supremum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $s\in\mathbb{R}$. The element $s$ satisfies the \emph{epsilon characterization of the supremum} of $A$ if and only if $s$ is an upper bound of $A$ and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that $s-\varepsilon<a$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $s\in\mathbb{R}$. The element $s$ satisfies the \emph{epsilon characterization of the supremum} of $A$ if and only if $s$ is an upper bound of $A$ and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $a\in A$ such that $s-\varepsilon<a$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A\subseteq\mathbb{R} \text{ and } s\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&s \text{ satisfies the epsilon characterization of } \sup A\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le s)\Bigr]
\land
\Bigl[\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists a\in A\;(s-\varepsilon<a)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A\subseteq\mathbb{R} \text{ and } s\in\mathbb{R}.\\

&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le s)\Bigr]
\land
\Bigl[\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists a\in A\;(s-\varepsilon<a)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A\subseteq\mathbb{R} \text{ and } s\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&s \text{ does not satisfy the epsilon characterization of } \sup A\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\exists x\in A\;(s<x)\Bigr]
\lor
\Bigl[\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall a\in A\;(a\le s-\varepsilon_0)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A\subseteq\mathbb{R} \text{ and } s\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&s \text{ does not satisfy the epsilon characterization of } \sup A\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\exists x\in A\;(s<x)\Bigr]
\lor
\Bigl[\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall a\in A\;(a\le s-\varepsilon_0)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes: The characterization fails either because $s$ is not an upper bound of $A$, or because $A$ remains at least some positive distance below $s$.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{EpsilonSupremum}(s,A)
=
\underbrace{\exists x\in A\;(s<x)}_{\text{upper-bound failure}}
\;\lor\;
\underbrace{\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall a\in A\;(a\le s-\varepsilon_0)}_{\text{positive gap below }s}.
\]
nodes.source_text: This condition says that $s$ caps the set from above while points of $A$ approach $s$ from below at every positive scale. The upper-bound clause prevents $A$ from crossing above $s$, and the epsilon clause prevents $s$ from floating strictly above the set. Geometrically, $s$ is a ceiling that the set presses against arbitrarily closely.

nodes.name: Bound
nodes.question: State the definition: Bound.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$, and let $b\in S$. The element $b$ is a \emph{bound} for $A$ if and only if $b$ is a uniform one-sided comparison point for all elements of $A$:
\[
\operatorname{Bound}(b,A)
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le b)\bigr]
\lor
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(b\le x)\bigr].
\]

\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le b)\bigr]
\lor
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(b\le x)\bigr].
\]

nodes.source_text: An upper bound caps a subset of an ordered structure from above, so every element of the subset fits beneath the chosen guard $u$. nodes.statement_display: Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set, $A\subseteq S$, and $m\in S$. The element $m$ is the \emph{minimum} of $A$ if and only if $m\in A$ and $m$ is a lower bound of $A$.

\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(m\in A \land \forall x\in A\;(m\le x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

\bigl(m\notin A \lor \exists x\in A\;(m\nleq x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[

nodes.failure_modes: Failure occurs either because $m$ is not a member of $A$, or because some element of $A$ lies strictly below $m$, violating the global lower-bound condition.
nodes.source_text: A minimum point both belongs to the set and sits at its absolute bottom: every other element rests above it in the ambient order. The definition splits into the membership requirement, ensuring the bound is realized, and the universal inequality that promotes the element from a mere lower bound to a genuine extremal. Failure arises if the candidate lies outside the set or if another element dips below it; geometrically, the set either has no realized floor at that point or its supposed floor is undercut elsewhere.

\[
\neg \operatorname{Maximum}(M,A)
=
\underbrace{(M \notin A)}_{\text{membership failure}}
\;\lor\;
\underbrace{\bigl(\exists x \in A\;(M < x)\bigr)}_{\text{domination failure}}.
\]
nodes.source_text: A maximum is an element of the set that simultaneously belongs to the set and dominates it under the ambient order. The domination clause guarantees that no point of $A$ lies above the maximum, so the element captures the extreme right edge of the subset. Failure occurs either when the supposed extremal is not actually part of the set or when another member protrudes farther to the right, showing the candidate was not truly maximal. In geometric terms, the maximum is the endpoint where the subset comes to rest when viewed along the ordering axis.

nodes.name: Nested Interval Property
nodes.question: State the theorem: Nested Interval Property.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(I_n)$ be a sequence of nonempty closed intervals in $\mathbb{R}$. If $I_{n+1}\subseteq I_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, then
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} I_n\neq\varnothing.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(I_n)$ be a sequence of nonempty closed intervals in $\mathbb{R}$. If $I_{n+1}\subseteq I_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, then
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} I_n\neq\varnothing.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall (a_n)\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\forall (b_n)\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\\
&\Bigl[
\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(a_n\le b_n)\bigr)
\land
\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;([a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq [a_n,b_n])\bigr)
\\
&\qquad\rightarrow
\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(x\in [a_n,b_n])
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}

\land
\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;([a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq [a_n,b_n])\bigr)
\\
&\qquad\rightarrow
\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(x\in [a_n,b_n])

\]

\\
&\qquad\land
\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;\exists n\in\mathbb{N}\;(x\notin [a_n,b_n])
\Bigr].

\]

nodes.name: Composition of Injections Is Injective
nodes.question: State the proposition: Composition of Injections Is Injective.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $f:A\to B$ and let $g:B\to C$. If $f$ is injective and $g$ is
injective, then $g\circ f:A\to C$ is injective.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $f:A\to B$ and let $g:B\to C$. If $f$ is injective and $g$ is
injective, then $g\circ f:A\to C$ is injective.

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Bigl(\forall a_1,a_2\in A\;(f(a_1)=f(a_2)\Rightarrow a_1=a_2)\Bigr)
\wedge
\Bigl(\forall b_1,b_2\in B\;(g(b_1)=g(b_2)\Rightarrow b_1=b_2)\Bigr) \\
&\quad\Rightarrow
\forall a_1,a_2\in A\;(g(f(a_1))=g(f(a_2))\Rightarrow a_1=a_2).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[

\wedge

&\quad\Rightarrow
\forall a_1,a_2\in A\;(g(f(a_1))=g(f(a_2))\Rightarrow a_1=a_2).
\end{aligned}
\]
